opus-5.5.text:
I think both errors are real, and they're not symmetric in the way people sometimes assume.

On the one hand, governments and wider society are still largely planning as if transformative AI is something for the 2040s or beyond, if they think about it at all. Even if you only put, say, a 10 or 20 percent chance on very capable systems arriving within the next five years, that's an enormous probability for something with stakes this large. We'd never accept that level of neglect for a 10 percent chance of a major pandemic or a financial collapse. So, from a portfolio point of view, society is badly underweighting the short-timelines scenarios, and I think that's the bigger collective mistake right now.

On the other hand, within the AI community, and particularly among people worried about AI risk, I see a fair bit of overconfidence in very short timelines. People extrapolate curves on benchmarks, or take the most bullish statements from lab leaders at face value, and end up with something like 70 or 80 percent confidence that AGI is two or three years away. I don't think the evidence supports that degree of certainty. Scaling has produced remarkable things, but we've also seen that some of the returns are harder-won than they looked. Pre-training scaling seems to have slowed, and a lot of recent progress has come from inference-time compute and reinforcement learning, which have different economics. They can get more expensive per unit of capability. There are genuine open questions about reliability, about agency over long horizons, about whether benchmark gains translate into real-world competence.

So the way I weigh them is something like: hold a genuinely wide distribution, and then act on the whole distribution rather than on its mode. Short timelines deserve far more attention than mainstream institutions give them, because that's where we're least prepared and where the work done now matters most. But individuals shouldn't make irreversible life decisions, or burn out, or abandon long-term projects, on the assumption that it's definitely happening by 2027. If it takes fifteen years, we'll need people and institutions who planned for that too.

There's also a reputational dimension. If the safety community stakes its credibility on a specific near-term date and that date passes, it becomes much harder to get people to take the risk seriously later, which might be exactly when it matters. So being honest about our uncertainty isn't just epistemically correct; it's strategically important. The message I'd want to get across is: this could come very soon, we're not ready for that, and we also don't know. All three of those things are true at once.

r001.rationale: The response says short timelines deserve more attention and preparation, while cautioning against acting as if AGI is definitely imminent; it explicitly holds uncertainty alongside preparedness.

r002.rationale: It calls society's underweighting of short-timeline scenarios the bigger collective mistake, while also acknowledging overconfidence among some AI-risk-focused people.

fable-5.1.text:
I think both of those are real failure modes, and I'd resist the temptation to pick just one of them as "the" problem. They're different mistakes, made by different people, and they have different costs.

Let me start with the neglect. If you look at how most governments and most of the public have been treating this, there's been a kind of assumption that transformative AI is something for the distant future, or for science fiction, and so the appropriate response is to wait and see. And I think that's just not a defensible position any more. Even if you're quite sceptical of the people saying it's three or four years away, you have to take seriously that a substantial fraction of the people who actually build these systems think it could be within a decade. When the people closest to a technology are saying something like that, the burden shifts. You don't need to believe them to think it's worth preparing. We prepare for pandemics and earthquakes without being certain they'll happen on any particular date. So the neglect side strikes me as a failure of basic risk management: not taking a plausible, high-stakes possibility seriously enough to even do the groundwork.

But then there's the overconfidence, and I don't want to let that off the hook either. There's a real tendency in this community to treat the short timelines as settled, to talk as if we know AGI is coming in 2027 or 2028, when what we actually have is a set of forecasts with very wide uncertainty and a track record of this field being wrong in both directions. And overconfidence has its own costs. It can lead people to make bad personal decisions, burning out, abandoning long-term plans. It can lead to a boy-who-cried-wolf dynamic where, if the predicted dates pass and nothing dramatic has happened, the people who were warning lose credibility right at the moment when it might really matter. And it can crowd out thinking about what to do in the worlds where this takes twenty or thirty years, which are still quite likely worlds.

So how do I weigh them? I think the honest answer is that the appropriate stance is something like: high uncertainty, with a non-trivial probability mass on very short timelines. And once you frame it that way, you can see that the two errors aren't symmetric in their consequences. If society prepares for a short-timeline world and it doesn't arrive, we've spent some money and attention, and much of that work, on governance, on safety research, on institutional capacity, is going to be useful anyway, just later. Whereas if we don't prepare and it does arrive, the costs could be enormous and very hard to reverse. That asymmetry means that, in terms of what the world should actually do, the neglect is the more dangerous error, even though the overconfidence is perhaps the more intellectually embarrassing one.

But I'd add one caveat, which is that I think the way to address the neglect is not with more overconfidence. The temptation is to say, well, people aren't listening, so we need to shout louder and make the claims more certain. I think that's a mistake. The argument that works, and the argument that's true, is the one from uncertainty: we don't know when this is coming, serious people think it could be soon, and that's exactly why we need to act now. You don't have to win the timeline debate to make that case. And I think it's more robust, because it doesn't collapse the moment one particular forecast turns out to be wrong.

r001.rationale: The response calls for high uncertainty with a non-trivial chance of very short timelines, and explicitly rejects treating short-timeline forecasts as settled or claiming more certainty to gain attention.

r002.rationale: It says that, for society’s actions, neglecting the possibility is the more dangerous error because the cost of failing to prepare could be enormous, while preparation has lower costs if AGI arrives later.

astra-6.text:
I think both are real problems, and they can reinforce each other. Governments and wider society can be paying far too little attention to the possibility of AGI arriving soon, while people within the AI discussion are much too confident that it will.

The key distinction is between believing that something will happen soon and believing that there’s a substantial chance it will happen soon. You don’t need to be confident about short timelines to think that preparing for them is urgent. If the consequences are sufficiently large, even a fairly modest probability can warrant serious attention—especially when preparation takes years.

But that doesn’t justify turning uncertainty into certainty for the sake of getting people to act. If you repeatedly say that AGI is just around the corner, and it doesn’t arrive, you risk undermining the credibility of the whole concern. And you may choose policies that only make sense under a very narrow picture of how things unfold.

So I’d want us to be much more serious about preparedness and much more modest about prediction. We should ask which actions would help across a range of timelines, and which preparations we would deeply regret not having made if progress turns out to be fast. That seems a better basis for policy than either complacency or a confident countdown.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes a substantial chance of near-term AGI, which can warrant preparation, from confidence that AGI will arrive soon, which it cautions against.

r002.rationale: It calls both neglect and overconfidence real problems but does not judge societal underestimation to be the bigger mistake.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different mistakes here, and we should be careful not to let concern about one push us into the other. Governments can be doing far too little to prepare for AGI arriving soon, while people working on AI can be much too confident that it will arrive soon.

You don’t need to think that short timelines are the most likely outcome to think they deserve serious preparation. If there’s a substantial chance of something happening that would transform the world, and preparing for it takes years, then waiting until you’re confident is a bad strategy. So I’m sympathetic to the criticism that governments and wider society haven’t taken this seriously enough.

But that’s different from saying we know when AGI will arrive. There’s a lot of uncertainty about what remains to be done, how quickly progress will continue, and whether the approaches that look promising now will get us all the way there. I’d be wary of treating a particular date as established, especially when so many decisions then get built around it.

What I’d like to see is greater urgency in preparation alongside greater humility in prediction. Those are perfectly compatible. We should be asking what we can do now that would put us in a better position across a range of possible timelines, rather than feeling that we have to settle the timeline question before we can act.

r001.rationale: The response says serious preparation is warranted even without treating short timelines as most likely, and separately cautions against treating a particular arrival date as established.

r002.rationale: It says both insufficient preparation and overconfidence are mistakes, but does not judge society’s underestimation to be the bigger mistake.
